body_markdown:
Oh, 1960. I wish I had been around at the time. Such cars! And instead of a bunch of SUVs defining luxury as is the case today, there were grand cars. *Cars* . Coupes, sedans, pillarless hardtops, convertibles!


And there were so many choices. Cadillac, Lincoln and Imperial were the top of the top, but there were also compelling choices from Chrysler, Buick, Oldsmobile and Mercury. But for the country club set, it really was only Caddy, Imperial, and Lincoln.


Jayson Coombes


Today’s Alaskan White Imperial Crown Southampton four-door hardtop was spotted by my friend Jayson Coombes at the April 11th Park Cities show in the Dallas metro area. This show always attracts really excellent cars, and the 2026 event was no exception.


Jayson Coombes


Jayson Coombes


In addition to the Imperial, there was also a gorgeous 1967 Buick Electra Limited four-door hardtop in a deep steel blue metallic, but that’s a car for another time. And I always love seeing Imperials, partly because they did not have the sales volume of Cadillac, which at the time was the 800-pound gorilla of domestic luxury fare.


Thomas Klockau


In fact, only 17,707 Imperials were built for the 1960 model year, and that is a shame, because they were wild and crazy and over the top, but also attractive and sumptuous. Advertising and brochures touted them as “America’s Most Carefully Built Car.”


Jayson Coombes


Sales literature enticed customers like this: “We present, with what we hope is allowable pride, the best automobile built in America in the last three decades. The Imperial of 1960. It is best in a number of ways. It has undeniable style. Impressive size and passenger space without mass or bulk.


Jayson Coombes


“It drives more easily. Its power steering and power brakes are unique in the motor world…acknowledged by unbiased experts as the best that motoring has offered…no other fine car maker has been able to match the poised, level comfort of Imperial’s Torsion-Aire ride.” And not to belabor the point, but it’s a pet peeve of mine: These are *Imperials* . Not Chryslers. If you call one a “Chrysler Imperial” you will sound just as foolish as if you called a Caddy a “General Motors Cadillac” or a 1961 Continental a “Ford Lincoln.” Now where was I?


Jayson Coombes


Oh yes, the luxury. I absolutely *love* the interiors on these. Luxury, but oh-so-Sixties futuristic! I especially like the blue interior on this example. Jayson said the leather was in perfect condition. I want Smithers to drive me to The Cellar for surf and turf in this while I enjoy a pre-dinner cocktail in the back seat. Ha!


Jayson Coombes


And bumps and bad roads were a mere detail when you rode in one of these, thanks to Chrysler Corporation’s vaunted torsion bar front suspension and the Imperial’s impressive 129-inch wheelbase. And by the way, the overall length of these was 226.3 inches. If you can parallel park this car, you can park anything!


I particularly liked the white paint combined with the marvelous blue leather interior, but there were far more brightly-hued colors available to the new Imperial buyer.


Jayson Coombes


Just a few of the compelling choices included Cedar Green, Light Mint, Dusk Mauve, Regal Red, Powdered Bronze, Beach Beige, Regent Ruby and Sheffield Silver.


Jayson Coombes


Under the hood was a 413-cubic-inch V-8, producing 350 horsepower at 4600 rpm and breathing through a Carter carburetor. The vaunted Chrysler TorqueFlite automatic transmission backed it up, controlled through pushbuttons on the instrument panel.


Jayson Coombes


The Crown was the mid-level model, above the Custom, but not quite as flossy as the top-of-the-line LeBaron. The Southampton four-door hardtop had an MSRP of $5647, a curb weight of 4765 pounds, and only 4510 were made. There was a Crown pillared sedan, also with a $5647 ask, but it was far less popular as only 1594 were sold.


Chrysler Corporation


A two-door hardtop and lush convertible rounded out the Crown line. The convertible is an especially rare bird even among 1960 Imperials, as only 618 of the $5774 luxury drop-tops were built.


Thomas Klockau


As so few Imperials were made, I’m really happy Jayson spotted this one! I did see a magnificent Regal Red ’60 Crown convertible at an Antique Automobile Club of America show in Moline, Illinois, about 15 years ago, but I don’t think I’ve seen one since!


Jayson Coombes
